lesson.title: Replacing Telnet: How SSH Locks Down Remote Access
lesson.summary: SSH is the encrypted protocol administrators use to remotely control machines, replacing plaintext protocols like Telnet with strong cryptographic protection for both the connection and the login itself.
lesson.body:
Before SSH, the standard way to log into a remote machine over a network was Telnet, and to a modern eye Telnet's design is alarming: every character typed, including usernames and passwords, was sent across the network as plain, readable text. Anyone positioned on the path between the two machines, or sharing the same local network, could simply watch the traffic and read a password straight out of it. Telnet was never built with an adversary in mind, and by the time the internet had grown large enough that untrusted networks were the norm rather than the exception, that design was a serious liability. SSH, the Secure Shell protocol, was created to replace it.

SSH is an application layer protocol that runs on top of TCP, conventionally on port 22, and its defining feature is that it establishes an encrypted, integrity protected channel before any login information is ever exchanged. As soon as a client connects, the two sides perform a key exchange to agree on a shared secret, which they use to encrypt everything that follows with a fast symmetric cipher. The details of exactly how two parties who have never met can agree on a shared secret over a network someone else might be watching, and why encrypting bulk traffic calls for a different kind of cryptography than establishing that secret does, are the subject of the next two chapters. For now, the important point is that by the time SSH asks for a username or password, the connection is already encrypted, so none of that information is exposed the way it was with Telnet.

SSH also uses public key cryptography for something Telnet never attempted at all: proving identity without ever transmitting a secret. Two identities need proving in an SSH session. First, the server proves itself to the client, using a host key, so the client can have some assurance it is really talking to the intended machine and not an impersonator; SSH clients typically remember a server's host key the first time they connect and warn loudly if it ever changes unexpectedly, a model often called trust on first use. Second, and just as important, the client can prove its own identity to the server using public key authentication instead of a password. In this setup, the person logging in holds a private key on their own machine, and the server has been given the matching public key ahead of time, usually placed in a file like authorized_keys. When the client connects, the server issues a challenge that only someone holding the correct private key could answer correctly, and the client answers it without the private key ever leaving their machine or crossing the network. An attacker who intercepts the entire exchange still cannot log in, because they never obtain the private key itself, only proof that someone else possesses it.

Put together, an administrator connecting to a cloud server today typically opens an SSH session, authenticates with a key pair rather than a password, and works in a terminal exactly as if they were sitting at the machine, all while every keystroke and every line of output is encrypted in transit. On the same network, the old Telnet approach would have handed a password to anyone with a packet sniffer within the first few seconds.
